23.0.big: Plants can't move, so they've evolved clever body parts and chemical signals to get water, light and nutrients, and to defend themselves.
points: This chapter covers the plant body (stems, roots, leaves), how water and sugar move, and how plants sense and respond to their world.

23.1.big: A plant has two systems: the shoot system above ground and the root system below. Both are built from a few basic tissues.
points: Shoot system: stems, leaves, flowers and fruits (flowers and fruits are the reproductive parts). Root system: anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals.
Meristematic tissue (a meristem) keeps dividing to make new cells. Everything else is permanent tissue (done dividing).

Apical meristem at the tips of shoots and roots makes the plant longer. Lateral meristem (the cambium) makes it wider. Intercalary meristem at the base of leaf blades and nodes lets grass regrow after you mow.

Three permanent tissue types: dermal tissue (outer covering, protection), vascular tissue (xylem carries water, phloem carries sugar), and ground tissue (everything else: photosynthesis, storage, support).
Simple tissues have one cell type. Complex tissues (like xylem and phloem) have several.

23.2.big: Stems hold the plant up, move water and sugar between roots and leaves, and sometimes store food.
points: Leaves attach at nodes. The space between is an internode. A leaf's stalk is the petiole. An axillary bud sits where a leaf meets the stem, and the apical bud is at the tip.
Dermal: the epidermis with a waxy cuticle, hair-like trichomes, and guard cells around stomata.

Vascular: xylem is made of tracheids and vessel elements (dead, hollow, with lignin walls). Phloem is made of sieve-tube cells plus companion cells. They run together in vascular bundles: scattered in monocots, in a ring in dicots.

Ground: parenchyma cells (the most common: photosynthesis and storage), collenchyma cells (flexible support, like celery strings), and sclerenchyma cells (stiff, dead support). Inside is the cortex and the center is the pith.

Primary growth = getting longer (apical meristem). Secondary growth = getting thicker. The vascular cambium makes secondary xylem (wood) inward and secondary phloem outward. The cork cambium makes bark and periderm, with lenticels (air holes).
Annual rings: each year adds one light, wide ring (spring) and one dark, narrow ring (late summer) of secondary xylem. Count pairs to find the age.

Modified stems: rhizome (underground horizontal stem, like ginger or iris), corm (solid underground stem, crocus), tuber (potato), bulb (onion), stolon and runner (strawberry), tendril (climbing), and thorn.
23.2.tip: Xylem goes up (water). Phloem goes everywhere (food). "Phloem = food."

23.3.big: Roots anchor the plant, soak up water and minerals, and often store food.
points: Tap root system: one big main root going deep (carrots, dandelions). Found in dicots. Fibrous root system: a shallow mat of many roots (grass, wheat). Found in monocots.

The root cap protects the growing tip and helps it push through soil. Behind it come three zones: dividing cells (meristem), the elongation zone, then the maturation zone with root hairs (tons of surface area for absorbing water).

Inside: the cortex stores starch. The endodermis has a waxy Casparian strip that forces water and minerals to go through cells, so the root can choose what gets in. Inside that is the pericycle (which makes side roots) and the vascular stele.
Modified roots: adventitious roots grow from stems or leaves (prop roots in corn, aerial roots in epiphytes like orchids).

23.4.big: Leaves are solar panels: flat and thin to catch light, with pores for gas exchange.
points: Parts: the flat blade is the lamina, the stalk is the petiole (a sessile leaf has none), and some leaves have small stipules at the base.
Venation (vein pattern): monocots have parallel veins. Dicots have net-like (reticulate) veins.
Phyllotaxy (leaf arrangement): alternate, opposite, or whorled (3+ at one node).
A simple leaf has one blade. A compound leaf is split into leaflets: palmately compound (spread from one point like fingers) or pinnately compound (along a midrib like a feather).
Inside: the mesophyll (palisade + spongy) does photosynthesis. Stomata are mostly on the underside, away from direct sun, to save water.
Adaptations: desert plants have spines and thick cuticles, conifers have needles with sunken stomata (cold and dry), and water lilies have stomata on top with big air spaces.

23.5.big: Water always moves from higher to lower water potential. Plants use that to pull water from soil to air with no pump.
points: Water potential (Ψw), measured in megapascals (MPa): Ψ = Ψs (solute) + Ψp (pressure) + Ψg (gravity) + Ψm (matric, the cling of water to surfaces). Pure water = 0.
Adding solutes makes Ψs more negative, so water flows in. Pressure (turgor) pushes Ψ up.
Transpiration: water evaporates out of stomata, which pulls a chain of water up the xylem (cohesion-tension). Soil Ψ > root Ψ > leaf Ψ > air Ψ.
Guard cells open stomata for CO₂ but close them when it's hot, dry or droughty (signaled by abscisic acid) to save water. High humidity slows transpiration.

Translocation: sugar moves in phloem from a source (where it's made or stored, like leaves) to a sink (where it's used or stored, like roots, fruits and growing tips). Sugar loaded into sieve tubes pulls water in, and that pressure pushes the sap along.
23.5.tip: Water potential: water slides downhill, from less negative to more negative.

23.6.big: Plants sense light, gravity and touch, and respond using hormones.
points: Light: photomorphogenesis = light shaping growth. Phytochrome switches between Pr and Pfr: red light → Pfr (active), far-red → Pr. That's how plants detect shade, time germination, and measure night length (photoperiodism). The light-absorbing part is a chromophore.
Blue light: phototropin causes phototropism (bending toward light). Cryptochrome helps set the daily clock.
Gravity: roots show positive gravitropism (grow down) and shoots show negative gravitropism (grow up). Heavy starch grains called statoliths settle to the bottom of cells to sense down.

Hormones: auxin (cell elongation, bending toward light, apical dominance), cytokinin (cell division, delays aging), gibberellin (GA) (stem lengthening, breaks seed dormancy, bigger fruit), abscisic acid (ABA) (stress hormone: closes stomata, keeps seeds dormant), ethylene (ripens fruit, leaf drop or abscission). Others: jasmonates (defense), oligosaccharins, strigolactones.

Touch: thigmomorphogenesis (wind makes stems shorter and thicker), thigmonastic (fast, non-directional response, like the Venus flytrap or Mimosa leaves folding), thigmotropism (directional growth from touch, like tendrils wrapping around).
Defense: thorns, waxy cuticle, toxins, bitter alkaloids against herbivores, and jasmonate signals that warn other leaves.
23.6.tip: Ethylene ripens fruit, which is why a banana in a paper bag ripens faster.

1.why: Hair roots are part of the root system, not the shoot system.

2.why: Roots absorb water, so without them the plant dries out.

3.why: Lateral meristem (vascular cambium) makes secondary xylem to thicken the stem.

4.why: Secondary xylem is finished, non-dividing (permanent) tissue. The others are meristems.

5.why: The root tip has an apical meristem, which adds length.

6.why: Grass regrows after mowing from intercalary meristems at the base of the blades.

8.why: The dye travels up with water, so the colored strands are xylem.

9.why: Simple tissue = one cell type, like parenchyma.

10.why: Complex tissue has several cell types working together.

11.why: Flowers and fruit are the reproductive parts.

12.why: Actively dividing cells at a root tip = meristem.

13.why: The stalk connecting leaf to stem is the petiole.

15.why: Xylem (tracheids, vessel elements) + phloem (sieve-tube cells, companion cells) = vascular tissue.

16.why: Thick lignin walls and hollow centers = xylem, which is vascular tissue.

17.why: Secondary growth = getting thicker, from the vascular cambium.

18.why: The cambium sits between secondary xylem (inside) and secondary phloem (outside).

19.why: Tree rings are layers of secondary xylem (wood).

20.why: Each year makes one wide ring and one narrow ring, so 4 + 4 rings = 4 years.

21.why: A rhizome is an underground horizontal stem, like an iris.

22.why: Cactus pads are flat, green, photosynthetic stems.

23.why: Parenchyma is the most common plant cell.

24.why: A dandelion's single deep main root is a taproot.

25.why: The taproot goes deep, so the weed is hard to pull out completely.

26.why: A cap on the tip protects it as it pushes through soil.

27.why: Cell division happens in the meristem just behind the root cap.

28.why: The endodermis (with its Casparian strip) controls what minerals get in.

29.why: The waxy Casparian strip (suberin) would stain deepest.

30.why: Plants that grow on other plants (epiphytes) use aerial roots.

31.why: Starch is stored in parenchyma of the cortex.

32.why: Fibrous = a large, dense network of roots.

33.why: Leaves drop at the petiole (the abscission zone).

38.why: CO₂ is fixed into glucose in the mesophyll first, then moves to the phloem.

40.why: Floating leaves with air chambers and a top cuticle = water lily.

41.why: You cut the petiole, the stalk that attaches the leaf.

43.why: Water clinging to the walls of xylem = matric potential.

44.why: More solute → water potential decreases → water moves in.

45.why: When it's hot, stomata close to save water.

46.why: Open stomata let water vapor out, which increases transpiration.

47.why: Sugar is loaded into the phloem's sieve elements to be carried away.

48.why: Sugar goes into the phloem: sieve-tube elements and companion cells.

49.why: Solute potential is also called osmotic potential.

50.why: Bends toward blue even without carotenoids, so it's phototropin.

52.why: Stems grow up, away from gravity (negative gravitropism).

55.why: Fruit gives off ethylene, which builds up in the bag.

57.why: Growing away from a stone it touches is directional growth from touch: thigmotropism.

58.why: Waxy cutin and suberin keep microbes out. The others target animals.

61.why: A circadian rhythm keeps going on schedule even in the dark.

62.why: Shallow roots = easy to uproot, and once out of the ground they can't regrow.

64.why: Apical = tips, length. Lateral = cambium, girth. Intercalary = nodes and leaf bases, length.

66.why: A is at the very tip of the shoot: apical meristem.

67.why: Anchors well (though not perfectly) and is a protected sink for stored starch.

68.why: Monocot stems: bundles scattered. Dicot stems: bundles in a ring.

69.why: Stomata let gases in and out, and guard cells open and close them. Without them, photosynthesis and transpiration stop.

71.why: The underside is in water, so stomata must be on the top.

72.why: The phloem is just under the bark in a ring. Cutting the ring stops sugar from reaching the roots.

73.why: As a dicot matures, the vascular cambium links the bundles and makes growth rings.

74.why: Taproot (carrot) = one deep root, in dicots. Fibrous (wheat) = shallow network, in monocots.

75.why: The cap protects the meristem and lubricates the path through soil.

76.why: Everything must cross the endodermis, where selection happens.

77.why: Underground food is hidden from animals, and the soil is steadier in temperature and moisture.

78.why: Deep taproot = reaches deep moist soil. Shallow fibrous = grabs water fast after a light rain.

80.why: Small leaflets are harder for big herbivores to find and eat.

81.why: The top gets more sun, so stomata there would lose more water.

82.why: Conifers (spruce, fir, pine) have needles with sunken stomata.

83.why: A leaf attaches at a node with a bud. A leaflet attaches to the midrib, not the stem.

84.why: Plant Ψ = −0.12 + (−2.3) = −2.42 MPa, more negative than the soil (−2.1), so water flows into the plant.

85.why: The circulatory system (heart, blood vessels): it moves water, nutrients and food around the body like xylem and phloem do.

86.why: Xylem cells (tracheids and vessel elements) die on purpose and leave behind empty, lignin-reinforced tubes. Those hollow tubes are what carry water.

87.why: Paint blocked the stomata, so no transpiration, so no pull to bring water up.

88.why: Water goes up the xylem, and sugar goes up and down the phloem.

89.why: Water only flows to lower Ψ. If the soil's Ψ drops below the plant's, water can't go in.

90.why: Stomata on both sides = both sides get sun. Mostly underneath = sun hits only the top.

91.why: In February, nights are long. Use long light periods (and red light to make active Pfr) to trick it into "long day".

92.why: Without gravity sensing, roots grow every which way and shoots don't head up.

93.why: Cold slows ripening, and airflow removes ethylene, which speeds ripening.

94.why: The trap only closes after repeated touches (two hairs touched), which an insect does but a raindrop doesn't.

95.why: Closing stomata keeps pathogens out, and ABA triggers it.

96.why: Shade means not enough light for photosynthesis. Big seeds have enough food to grow out of the shade.

97.why: Water moves soil → plant. Dry soil has a lower Ψ than wet soil. Stomata close in drought.

98.why: Past 27 °C, stomata close to save water, so transpiration drops.

99.why: Humid air narrows the difference in water vapor between leaf and air, so less evaporation.

101.why: Spray ABA to trigger drought protection (closing stomata) ahead of time.

102.why: Red light alone gave 95%. Red then far-red undid it (50%, same as dark). So red promotes germination.

103.why: Red makes active Pfr, far-red reverses it. After an hour, Pfr has already started the germination signals, so far-red can't undo it.

104.why: Open cuts let pathogens in. Sealing blocks them.

105.why: Plants with jasmonate did better against both fungi and moths, so it protects broadly.

106.why: It blooms with long nights (short days), so it's a short-day plant and would bloom when days are short, like February.

107.why: The motion continues in the dark (so no light needed) but the waves shrink, as if a clock molecule wears out.

108.why: Seedlings in the dark stretch to find light (8 mm vs 3 mm): elongation from lack of light.

109.why: More gibberellin = longer internodes, which gives the big grapes more room.
